title: ISTE Endorses Speech & Debate
author: Stefan Bauschard
summary: Stefan Bauschard uses the International Society for Technology in Education's rebranding moment — ISTE quietly swapped 'Technology' for 'Transforming' in its name — as a launching point for arguing that speech and debate is the most underrecognized pathway to producing the AI-ready graduates ISTE's new framework describes. ISTE's new 'Profile of an AI-Ready Graduate' centers on judgment, not tool fluency: the capacity to decide in a specific moment what information to trust, what argument to follow, and what action to take. Bauschard argues this is a precise description of what competitive debate already develops systematically — students must synthesize information rapidly, evaluate argument quality under pressure, and communicate with clarity to a hostile audience. The article connects to a growing recognition that the cognitive skills most resistant to AI replacement are the ones that have always mattered in traditional debate: evaluating evidence, constructing reasoning chains, adapting to counterargument, and communicating persuasively. Bauschard closes with a call for educators to treat debate and speech not as extracurricular enrichment but as core curriculum for an AI-saturated world.
points: ISTE's rebranding from 'Technology in Education' to 'Transforming Education' signals a fundamental shift: the organization that spent forty years putting devices into classrooms has concluded that the tool is not the point — and that what matters is the transformation the tool enables.

ISTE's 'Profile of an AI-Ready Graduate' centers on judgment, not tool fluency, making it a description of debate skills: the capacity to evaluate information quality, reason under pressure, and communicate persuasively to skeptical audiences.

The skills competitive debate systematically develops — rapid synthesis, argument evaluation, counterargument response, evidence assessment — are precisely the skills that AI cannot currently replicate and that the AI-saturated workplace will reward most.

Bauschard's implicit argument is that the 'AI-readiness' conversation in education needs to shift from curriculum content (what do students need to know about AI?) to cognitive development (what capacities do students need to navigate an AI-saturated world?).

The case for debate as core curriculum rather than extracurricular enrichment rests on the claim that deliberate adversarial argument practice is the most direct path to judgment — and judgment is what will distinguish graduates in a world where content knowledge is increasingly commoditized.
quotes: As of June 28 [ ], it stands for the International Society for Transforming Education. CEO Richard Culatta’s explanation was blunt: we can’t keep doing assessment the way we used to [ ], can’t keep teaching the way we used to, and a name about the tool no longer describes the work.

Debate is one of the last places in a teenager’s life where the “problematic not to use your own mind” muscle gets loaded to failure on purpose. We have endless conversations about teaching students to use AI well.

They are self-directed learners by necessity, which is precisely the disposition that lets a student treat an AI tutor as an accelerant instead of a crutch. The framework wants students who can clarify a challenge, generate options, and evaluate solutions.

A debater who has spent a season getting punished in-round for reading a weak card does not take a confident-sounding AI summary at face value. They’ve been burned by fluent, authoritative text before — and that scar tissue is the whole point.

The debater takes 40-90 minutes of clash, decides which two arguments actually matter, collapses everything else, and re-pitches the entire round to the specific person holding the ballot — in five minutes. That is synthesis under pressure, which is the only kind of synthesis the real world ever actually asks for.
You cannot tell when an AI’s argument is weak unless you can build a strong one. You cannot catch a dishonest synthesis unless you’ve sweated through honest ones.
